title: Protest, freedom of expression and the public-private law divide
gist: The UK Supreme Court acquitted Animal Rebellion protesters who blocked a private dairy access road by ruling that public-nuisance offences under the Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Act 2022 require an actual public right, not merely licensed access to private land — and it did so almost entirely without invoking the Human Rights Act, which the author reads as a sign courts are 'proofing' protest law against a possible future repeal of that Act.

themes.theme: The case: Animal Rebellion at the Müller dairy works

insights.claim: Animal Rebellion activists who blocked a private access road at the Müller UK dairy works in the Midlands were prosecuted for public nuisance under the new Section 78 offence created by the Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Act 2022, which also abolished the old common-law offence of public nuisance.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
entities: Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Act 2022
insights.so_what: Establishes the specific statutory hook prosecutors used against the protest, which the case would go on to test.
insights.quote: The protesters blocked what was a private access road at the Müller UK dairy works in the Midlands. They were prosecuted as a public nuisance under the new offence in Section 78
insights.locator: The protesters blocked what was a private access road

insights.claim: The defendants successfully applied to have the prosecution discontinued on the basis that they could not be prosecuted for obstructing 'the public in the exercise or enjoyment of a right' when the protest occurred on private land, and the trial judge halted the trial on that basis.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: Shows the case turned on a narrow but consequential legal distinction between public and private land from the outset.
insights.quote: The judge halted the trial. The legal point was simple: how could they be prosecuted for obstructing “the public in the exercise or enjoyment of a right” when the protest was on private land?

insights.claim: The Court of Appeal initially sided with the prosecution, ruling that the public has a right to attend places offered to the public at large even where subject to conditions, meaning the private road counted as available to the public and the offence was made out.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: Shows the lower appellate court took a broader, more prosecution-friendly reading before the Supreme Court intervened.
insights.quote: the public at large have a right to attend places and events or to use facilities and services which are offered to the public at large
insights.locator: The Court of Appeal then sided with the prosecution

insights.claim: The UK Supreme Court chose to hear the case despite rarely accepting appeals from the criminal division of the Court of Appeal, and its majority sided with the protesters against both the prosecution and the Court of Appeal's judges.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: Signals the Supreme Court viewed the underlying legal question as significant enough to warrant a rare criminal appeal.
insights.quote: The Supreme Court does not hear many appeals from the criminal division of the Court of Appeal, but it chose to hear this one.
insights.locator: The Supreme Court does not hear many appeals

themes.theme: The legal principle: licence versus right

insights.claim: The Supreme Court's core reasoning was that having permission or ability to enter private land creates only a licence, which can be withdrawn, not a public right — so blocking a private road cannot be prosecuted as obstructing a public right.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: Clarifies the durable legal distinction the ruling establishes for future protest prosecutions on nominally 'public-facing' private land.
insights.quote: Having a permission, or even an ability, to enter private land does not create a right. It is instead a mere licence, which can be withdrawn.
insights.locator: The relevant legal principle was simple

insights.claim: The right to use the 'King's Highway' is one of the oldest rights in English common law, held by all members of the public and not set out in statute, and it underpins the distinction the Supreme Court drew between public and private space in this case.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: Grounds the modern ruling in an ancient common-law concept, showing legal continuity rather than novel doctrine.
insights.quote: one of the rights held by all members of the public is to use what is quaintly known as the “King’s Highway”. This is one of the oldest rights in English law.
insights.locator: There are rights which only a few people have

insights.claim: The private road in question, Pointon Way, was found not to be part of the King's Highway, meaning it fell outside the class of rights the public-nuisance offence was designed to protect.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: Provides the concrete factual anchor for how the abstract public/private distinction applied to this specific site.
insights.quote: Pointon Way, the lane in question, was a private road and not part of the King’s Highway.
insights.locator: Pointon Way, the lane in question

insights.claim: One Supreme Court justice suggested a broader offence could be based on interference with the public's general 'right' to go about their business, but the majority rejected this as too vague and insufficiently certain for use in criminal law.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: Shows the majority deliberately chose a narrower, more predictable rule over an expansive one that could have made more protest activity prosecutable.
insights.quote: the majority rightly did not go with such vague wishy-washiness. Such an offence could not be sufficiently certain in its scope. The courts had to be strict in how they interpreted rights, especially in criminal cases.

insights.claim: The Supreme Court noted the prosecution could have properly charged the protesters under another limb of the new public nuisance offence, or under aggravated trespass — an offence specifically created for incidents on private land — implying police and the Crown Prosecution Service picked the wrong charge.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: Highlights a practical enforcement failure: protesters were acquitted not because their conduct was lawful in principle, but because prosecutors chose the wrong statutory tool.
insights.quote: In their eagerness to prosecute, the police and the Crown Prosecution Service had blundered in the offence they selected.
insights.locator: The Supreme Court also pointed out the deficiencies

insights.claim: The Human Rights Act was cited only in passing in the Supreme Court's judgment, and its provisions were not expressly invoked in deciding the case, even though a fundamental rights issue — freedom of expression and protest — was at stake.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: Marks a notable shift in how the UK's top court is resolving rights-based protest cases, relying on domestic common law rather than the HRA framework.
insights.quote: The Human Rights Act is cited only in passing, in relation to an earlier case. Its provisions were not expressly invoked by the Supreme Court in this case.
insights.locator: But what is perhaps most interesting

insights.claim: The author interprets the Supreme Court deciding a freedom-of-expression and protest case on common law and statutory construction, rather than the Human Rights Act, as the courts effectively 'proofing' protest-rights law against any future repeal of human rights legislation.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: Suggests UK courts are building rights protections into resilient common-law doctrine, reducing the practical stakes of political threats to repeal the Human Rights Act.
insights.quote: It is almost as if the courts are proofing the law against any repeal of human rights legislation.
